latin.323:
§. II.
Inter priores de S. Coena Controversias Protestanticæs, prima omnium est de Interpretatione verborum Institutionis Coenae horisticorum seu definitivorum: Hoc est corpus meum: Quae ut tanto amplior pinguiorque appareret, ab altera Protestantium parte in duas nequicquam discerpta est, quarum priori quaeritur: Num literaliter vel κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν? Posteriori: Num propriè, an verò impropriè verba S. Coenae, vel potiùs propositiones: Hoc est corpus meum, & Hic est Sanguis meus, capiendae sint.
latin.324: Ex una duas sic Controversias nequicquam constitui, ad oculum patet, si observetur: Τὸ κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν Propositionem accipere, triplici modô contingere posse, (1.) uti verba retineas, idque vel formaliter, vel aequipollenter, aequipollentia scil. formali, hoc est ea, quâ à formaliter retentis ne conceptu quidem distinguantur aequipollentia. (2.) Sensum verborum genuinum nativumque sequaris. (3.) Sensum verborum velis esse proprium.
latin.325: Enimverò de prioribus duabus significationibus τοῦ capiendi verba κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν, vel τῷ ῥητῷ retinendi, litigium nullum inter Protestantes, utrâque parte persuasâ, tam Verba formalia & aequipollentia quaecunque, quàm verborum utrorumque sensum genuinum, h. e. semper unum eundemque, verum illum mentique Christi convenientem, tenendum servandumque esse, ut sola tertia in dubio maneat & controversa. Confirmatur: scil. literalem verborum, in propositione spectatorum, controversum sensum ad hoc recidere: Num Sensus literalis, proprius, an verò improprius sit?
latin.326: Quia literalis alicujus propositionis, etiam Biblicae, sensus, proprio impropriôque latior existit, & ad hos, etiam aequè perspicuos, perinde extensus: neque enim sensus alicujus propositionis biblicae minus literalis, i. e. minùs verus genuinus & dicentis menti ac intentioni minus conformis, quin & minus perspicuus, remanet, si impropria, quam si propria facta sit praedicatio, litera propositionis, unà cum perspicuitate sua, Improprietati non minùs, quàm Proprietati, obnoxia, vel ab ista non minus quam ab hac, afficienda. Unde rectissimè Scherzerus: Ad perspicuitatem, inquit, pertinet omnino sensus literalis seu Logicus, i. e. quem Spiritus S. per se primo & proximè intendit, sive propriis verbis, sive figurato sermonis genere efferatur. Si enim sensus literalis solùm propriis verbis proferretur, plures orationes Biblicae nullum haberent sensum literalem, quod absurdum, System. Theol. loc. 1. §. 24. p. m. 24. in fin.
latin.327: Cui adstipulatur, etiam quà applicationem ad propositionem S. Coenae de qua nunc quaeritur, Sebastian. Schmidius Tract. de principiis seu Fundamentis praesentiae corporis & Sanguinis Christi in S. Coena cap. 3. §. 17. Literalis sensus, seu τὸ ῥητόν, ait, est is sensus, quem verba ipsa immediatè, consideratis omnibus circumstantiis, reddunt: ubi libenter admittimus τὸ ῥητόν seu literalem sensum non tantùm esse, quem verba propriè sumta dare possunt, sed etiam quem tropicè accepta subministrant. Ut adeò literalem istum sensum, modò, verba propriè accepta, modò, verba tropicè usurpata, suggerant. Sic literalem sensum habent non tantum verba Petri, Matth. 16. vers. 16. Tu es Filius Dei viventis, sed & verba ipsius Domini Jesu, Joh. 6. vers. 51. Ego sum panis vivus; licet hic tropus sit, ibi nullus. Et hactenus inter nos & Calvinianos nihil erit controversiae, p. 18. in fin. & 19.
latin.328: Ibidem, postquam de literali sensu verborum, extra propositionem spectatorum, i. e. de horum proprietate, Reformatis nunquam non concedenda, frustraque quaedam subjecisset, etiam, contra omnem Reformatorum mentem, asseruisset, eos literalem verborum S. Coenae sensum, à se retentum, mystico solì seu allegorico oppositum velle, cùm hunc oppositum velint omni falso minusque genuino, vel cuivis à mente loquentis Christi & huius immediata intentione, abhorrenti, sponte suâ agnoscit, omnem disputationem de sensu literali verborum Coenae retento, vel minùs retento, quam Protestantes inter se agitant, huc recurrere: An verba (prout nempe propositionem Christi absolvunt) Hoc est corpus meum, propriè, an verò impropriè, capienda sint? Discrimen, inquit, (inter nos & Calvinianos) hôc loco est illud quod Calviniani à proprietate verborum, ubi non deberent, recedunt, reliquae vero sententiae Literam se sequi & premere confitentur: Quare verborum S. Coenae Hoc est Corpus meum, Hoc est sanguis meus (puta quatenus non singula in se verba considerantur, utpote eatenus propria sua significatione à Reformatorum nemine exuenda privandaque unquam, sed quatenus integram Christi propositionem conficiunt, de cujus proprietate & improprietate controvertitur) ῥητόν, litera, seu literalis sensus, is est (scil. Lutheranis) cùm verba ista omnia in propriis suis significationibus relinquuntur, nec ad tropum, quicunque ille tandem sit, disceditur. p. 19. in fin. & 20. Sic verò Reformatos Lutherani habent consentientes, cum hoc solùm negent Reformati: Verba Christi prout propositionem constituunt, sensumque suum literalem, verum genuinum, i. e. menti dicentis Christi exactè respondentem, propositioni impropriae propriaeque juxta communem, obtinent, propriè accipi. Vel, ut clariùs loquar: Propositiones has: Hoc est Corpus meum, & hic est sanguis meus, (in literali i. e. genuino veroque sensu suo acceptas) proprias negant esse Reformati (Vid. Gom. Tom. 3. Diff. 35. thes. 10.) quas vice versâ proprias contendunt Lutherani, alioquin, nullô omnino discrimine hîc à Reformatis distincti, vel distinguendi.

pass_a.323: §. II. Among the prior Protestant Controversies on the Sacred Supper, the first of all is on the Interpretation of the horistic or definitive words of the Institution of the Supper: This is my body: which, that it might appear so much the ampler and fatter, has been needlessly torn by one Protestant party into two, of which the prior asks: Whether literally or κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν? The posterior: Whether properly, or rather improperly, the words of the Sacred Supper — or rather the propositions This is my body and This is my Blood — are to be taken.
pass_a.324: That two Controversies are thus needlessly constituted from one is plain to the eye, if it be observed that to take a Proposition κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν can happen in a threefold way: (1) that you retain the words, and that either formally or equipollently — by formal equipollence, that is, such that the equipollents are not distinguished even in concept from those formally retained; (2) that you follow the genuine and native sense of the words; (3) that you wish the sense of the words to be proper.
pass_a.325: But on the prior two significations of taking the words κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν, or of retaining them τῷ ῥητῷ, there is no litigation among Protestants, both parties being persuaded that both whatever formal and equipollent Words, and the genuine sense of both sorts of words — that is, always one and the same, the true one agreeing with Christ’s mind — are to be held and kept, so that only the third remains in doubt and controversial. It is confirmed: namely that the controversial literal sense of the words, viewed in the proposition, reduces to this: Whether the Literal Sense is proper, or rather improper?
pass_a.326: Because the literal sense of any proposition, even a Biblical one, is wider than the proper and the improper, and is equally extended to these, even equally perspicuous: nor does the sense of any biblical proposition remain less literal — that is, less true, genuine, and conformed to the speaker’s mind and intention, nay and less perspicuous — if the predication has been made improper than if proper, the letter of the proposition, together with its perspicuity, being no less liable to Impropriety than to Propriety, or to be affected by the former no less than by the latter. Whence most rightly Scherzer: To perspicuity, he says, belongs altogether the literal or Logical sense, i.e. what the Holy Spirit by Himself first and proximately intends, whether it be uttered in proper words or in a figurative kind of speech. For if the literal sense were brought forth only in proper words, many Biblical orations would have no literal sense, which is absurd — System of Theology, locus 1, §. 24, p. m. 24 at the end.
pass_a.327: To whom Sebastian Schmidius also agrees, even as to application to the proposition of the Sacred Supper now in question — Treatise on the principles or Foundations of the presence of the body and Blood of Christ in the Sacred Supper, ch. 3, §. 17. The Literal sense, or τὸ ῥητόν, he says, is that sense which the words themselves immediately render, all circumstances considered: where we gladly admit that τὸ ῥητόν or the literal sense is not only what words taken properly can give, but also what they furnish when accepted tropically. So that that literal sense is suggested now by words accepted properly, now by words used tropically. Thus not only Peter’s words, Matt. 16:16, You are the Son of the living God, have a literal sense, but also the Lord Jesus’s own words, John 6:51, I am the living bread — though here there is a trope, there none. And thus far there will be no controversy between us and the Calvinists, p. 18 at the end & 19.
pass_a.328: In the same place, after he had needlessly added some things on the literal sense of the words viewed outside the proposition — i.e. on their propriety, never not to be conceded to the Reformed — and had even asserted, against the whole mind of the Reformers, that they want the literal sense of the Sacred Supper’s words retained by them opposed only to the mystical or allegorical, whereas they want that opposite to every false and less genuine sense, or to whatever abhors from the mind of speaking Christ and His immediate intention, he spontaneously acknowledges that every dispute on the literal sense of the Supper’s words retained or less retained, which Protestants agitate among themselves, recurs hither: Whether the words (namely as they complete Christ’s proposition) This is my body are to be taken properly, or rather improperly? The difference, he says, (between us and the Calvinists) in this place is that the Calvinists recede from the propriety of the words where they ought not, while the remaining opinion confesses that it follows and presses the Letter: Wherefore of the Sacred Supper’s words This is my Body, This is my blood (namely insofar as the several words are not considered in themselves — for so far their proper signification is never to be stripped or deprived by any of the Reformers — but insofar as they complete Christ’s whole proposition, on whose propriety and impropriety the controversy turns) the ῥητόν, letter, or literal sense is (namely for Lutherans) when all those words are left in their proper significations and there is no departure to a trope, whichever it finally be. p. 19 at the end & 20. Thus the Lutherans have the Reformed consenting, since the Reformed deny only this: that Christ’s words, as they constitute the proposition and obtain their literal, true, genuine sense — i.e. exactly answering the mind of speaking Christ — according to the common rule for an improper and a proper proposition, are taken properly. Or, that I may speak more clearly: these Propositions This is my Body and this is my blood (accepted in their literal, i.e. genuine and true sense) the Reformed deny to be proper (see Gomarus, Tom. 3, Disp. 35, thesis 10), which conversely the Lutherans contend to be proper — otherwise here distinguished, or to be distinguished, from the Reformed by no difference at all.

323: §. II. Of the earlier Protestant Supper controversies, the first is how to read the definitive Institution words: This is my body.
One party has needlessly torn that question in two: whether literally / κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν, and whether the propositions This is my body / This is my Blood are taken properly or improperly.
324: That one fight should not be counted as two is plain once you see that taking a proposition κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν can mean three things.
First: keep the words — formally, or by formal equipollents that do not even differ in concept.
Second: follow the words’ genuine native sense.
Third: want that sense to be proper.
325: On the first two meanings Protestants have no lawsuit: both sides hold the formal (and equipollent) words, and one genuine sense that fits Christ’s mind.
Only the third stays doubtful and contested.
So the disputed “literal” sense of the words in the proposition reduces to this: is that literal sense proper, or improper?
326: A biblical proposition’s literal sense is wider than proper vs improper, and stretches equally to both with equal clarity.
An improper predication does not make the sense less literal, less true, or less matched to the speaker’s intent — the letter is open to impropriety no less than to propriety.

Scherzer puts it best: the literal or logical sense is what the Spirit first and proximately intends, whether in proper words or figurative speech; otherwise many biblical sayings would have no literal sense at all (Syst. Theol. I.§.24).
327: Sebastian Schmidius agrees for the Supper proposition itself: the literal sense / τὸ ῥητόν is what the words immediately yield when all circumstances are weighed.
He gladly allows that τὸ ῥητόν covers not only words taken properly but also words taken tropically.

So Peter’s You are the Son of the living God (Matt. 16:16) and Christ’s I am the living bread (John 6:51) are both literal — though only the second is a trope — and thus far there is no quarrel with the Calvinists (pp. 18–19).
328: After needless talk of word-propriety outside the proposition — which the Reformed never refuse — Schmidius himself grants that the whole Protestant fight over a retained or less-retained “literal” sense of the Supper words comes back to one question: as they complete Christ’s proposition, are This is my body taken properly or improperly?

For Lutherans the ῥητόν of This is my Body / This is my blood (as one whole proposition, not the several words stripped of their own proper sense) is when every word stays in its proper signification and no trope is admitted.

The Reformed deny only that those propositions, taken in their genuine literal sense, are proper (Gomarus, Tom. 3, Disp. 35, th. 10); Lutherans contend they are — otherwise the two sides would not differ here at all.
Stop before §. III (Reformed proofs that the definitive Supper propositions are improper — generic/specific arguments).
